What’s wrong with my pint?

Sixteen things that can be wrong with a pint, when each of them belongs there anyway, and what you can actually say at the bar.

There is butter in your pint.

Not much, but it is there, somewhere behind the hops, and once you have noticed it you cannot stop noticing it.

That is diacetyl, and it is the most useful fault in beer, because it arrives by two unrelated routes. It can come from the brewery, where the yeast was taken off the beer before it had finished clearing up after itself. Or it can come from the pub, out of a draught line that has not been cleaned properly, where bacteria make the same compound from scratch. Jess Keller Poole set both causes side by side writing for Hop Culture in 2020. Same taste, same word. One of them may have happened three months ago and four hundred miles away, and the other last Tuesday, nine feet from where you are standing. Nothing in the glass tells you which.

It may also be nothing at all. A little butter belongs in a Bohemian pilsner, and Thomas Barnes’s Complete Beer Fault Guide says the same of a sweet stout or an English IPA. So the useful version of this is not a diagnosis. It is a pattern: butter in one pint tells you nothing, and butter in two or three unrelated beers in the same pub is worth asking the bar to look at.

That is the whole subject in one flavour. A fault is only a fault in the wrong place, and the taste on its own will not always tell you where it came from.

Every list of beer faults is written for somebody, and the somebody is almost never you. The brewers’ lists are for people who can change what happens in a tank. The cellar manuals are for people who can clean a line. This one is for the person holding the glass, in the only order that helps at the bar: the everyday word first, the chemistry second, because nobody has ever thought isovaleric acid before thinking old socks.

The sixteen

Antiseptic, or TCP

A hospital note, sharp and chemical, sometimes with a numbing edge. Chlorophenols, and it takes almost nothing: Barnes puts it at three to forty micrograms a litre, which is why a trace ruins a whole glass. The Norfolk line cleaning firm Avani Solutions, who sell the service and should be read with that in mind, give the British cellar version, chlorine from cleaning products meeting phenols already in the beer. It belongs nowhere, in Barnes’s one word.

What to do. Tell the bar, and name the beer. If it came from the cellar rather than the brewery it will be on every pint off that line, which is something they can check and you cannot.

Butter

Butter, buttered popcorn, butterscotch, sometimes a slick feel rather than a taste. The beginning of this piece is about it. Where it belongs is a longer list than most people expect: Barnes allows low levels in Bohemian pilsner, English pale ales, Scottish ales, brown porters, sweet and oatmeal stouts and English IPA. Whether you can taste it at all is genetic. Some find it at ten micrograms a litre and some never find it.

What to do. One buttery pint tells you nothing. Two or three unrelated beers in the same pub is the pattern worth mentioning.

Cardboard, or wet paper

Stale and papery, a shoe box or a damp envelope. Low down, people reach for other words instead: inky, library, old books. This is oxidation, and the compound named for it, trans-2-nonenal, has one of the lowest thresholds in Barnes’s guide. It shows up first in pale, light, weaker beers, where there is nothing to hide behind. Never right as cardboard, although oxidation taken further gives the sherry and leather that belong in an old ale or a barleywine.

What to do. Ask how long it has been on. A cask takes in air the moment it is broached, so it has days rather than weeks. A keg under gas does not.

Cheese, or old socks

Blue cheese, stale laundry, feet. Isovaleric acid, out of hops that oxidised in storage rather than anything that happened in the pub. Everybody can taste it, though sensitivity varies by orders of magnitude. It belongs nowhere: Barnes opens the lambic exception, where brewers do use aged hops, and then closes it, because they are aged long enough that the cheese has gone.

What to do. Nothing, and nothing the bar can do either. You can still say you would rather not drink it.

Clove, smoke and spice

Clove, pepper, sometimes bacon or sticking plaster, depending which phenol it is and how much. Phenols come from yeast, from certain malts and from contamination, and the three are not distinguishable in the glass. This one belongs very often. Barnes expects low to medium clove in German wheat and rye beers and in Belgian ales, and a hefeweizen without it is the one with the problem.

What to do. Check the style before complaining. Clove in a wheat beer is the yeast doing its job.

Damp cellar

Mushrooms, mildew, old books, a basement. Musty character, usually traced to fungi in lines left standing or in insulation that has failed, and with one of the lowest thresholds on this list. It can also come from the malt or the brewing equipment, and that part was settled long before the cellar. It belongs nowhere.

What to do. Tell the bar. If it is the lines it will not be confined to your glass, which is the quickest thing for them to check.

Green apple

Green apple, bruised apple, sometimes emulsion paint. Acetaldehyde, which every fermentation makes on the way to alcohol and healthy yeast then takes back up. Beer that left before the yeast had finished is the usual explanation, with oxidation and bacterial spoilage behind it. It belongs almost nowhere, although Mark Dredge names one to learn it from: open a Budweiser and there is a little in it, adding a fresh, crisp flavour.

What to do. Say so if it is strong. Neither you nor the bar can tell which of the three causes you are tasting, but a pint you do not want to drink is still a pint you can mention.

Marmite, or soy sauce

Marmite, soy sauce, brothy and meaty, and at the top of the scale burnt rubber. This is autolysis: yeast cells dying weeks or months after they settled out and, in Barnes’s words, literally spilling their guts into the beer. The comparison is not a figure of speech. Marmite is made by doing the same thing on purpose, with heat. It belongs in one narrow place, extremely low, in strong aged bottle-conditioned beers and old ales especially.

What to do. Nothing, and nothing the bar can do. Age and how warm the beer has been kept settled this before the bottle reached you.

Metallic

Coins, blood, rust, a tinny edge that stays after the beer has gone. Barnes files the cause as contamination and gives the same one-word answer on where it belongs: never.

What to do. Mention it, although it is one of the harder ones for a pub to chase. Check first that it is not the glass, or whatever you drank before it.

Nail varnish, or pear drops

One ester read twice. Low down it is pear drops and fruit; high up it is solvent and nail varnish remover, and the line between them is degree rather than kind. Esters at sensible levels are a large part of what makes ale taste of anything, and Barnes expects them across English, Belgian and German ales. As solvent, never.

What to do. Nothing in the pub. It is worth knowing only so that pear drops in a Belgian ale does not get reported as a fault.

Onion and garlic

Exactly what it says, and unmistakable once noticed. This is where the guides part company. the Brewers Association files it as an off-flavour and then notes that it comes off the hops and is not always unwelcome. Barnes says detectable onion or garlic is never appropriate. Same compound, different reader. At very low levels the same chemistry feeds the sulphury note some pale lagers are supposed to have.

What to do. If it is strong enough to argue about, it is strong enough to say so and leave.

Rotten eggs

Eggs, drains. Hydrogen sulphide, from yeast or from infection, and the one fault here that sometimes walks away while you watch. Very low sulphury notes from yeast are accepted in some light lagers and in pale hoppy English ales. Anything you would call noticeable is a defect.

What to do. Wait a minute. It is volatile and some of it leaves the glass, so a note that fades may simply have blown off. If it is still there, say so.

Skunk

Nothing to do with hygiene, brewing or age. It is light. Wavelengths below 520 nanometres break down hop compounds and liberate a mercaptan close to the one a skunk uses, and Barnes puts the timescale at thirty seconds to two minutes. It belongs nowhere, although he adds the sting: it is so common in green-bottled imported lager that drinkers have learned to expect it, and some believe it is the recipe.

What to do. This is the one you can settle in a shop. Barnes measures the packaging: amber glass lets through about five per cent of the ultraviolet, green about eighty, and clear about ninety. A can lets through none. Jess Keller Poole makes the same point for drinkers.

Sweetcorn

Cooked sweetcorn, canned vegetables, sometimes tomato juice. Dimethyl sulphide, which comes out of the malt and is driven off by a vigorous boil. It belongs more often than people think, in light lagers, German pilsner, maibock and cream ale. Stuart Howe, quoted by Mark Dredge, gives the reason it favours pale lager: the gentler kilning of lager malt leaves more of the precursor behind.

What to do. Nothing, and in a pilsner you may be tasting the style rather than a mistake.

Tart, or yoghurt

Clean sourness, lemon, sour cream. Lactic acid, made by bacteria, and the clearest case in beer of a fault and a feature being the same molecule. Barnes accepts very low lactic sourness in dry stout, expects medium to high levels in Berliner weisse, and expects both lactic and a little acetic in Belgian sour ales.

What to do. Ask what it is before deciding it is wrong. Sourness in a bitter is spoilage. The same sourness in a Flanders red is the reason it costs more.

Vinegar

Sharp, cidery, the back of the throat. Acetic acid, from bacteria and usually from air. Its threshold is high compared with the rest of this list, so by the time you can taste it there is plenty of it. It belongs in a narrow but real set, and Barnes expects low acetic sourness in Flanders red, Flanders brown and lambic.

What to do. In anything else, send it back. Vinegar is one of the few here that nobody will argue with you about.

At the bar

You do not have to name the compound, work out whether it came from a fermenting vessel or a length of tubing, or settle an argument between a brewer and a publican before asking somebody to check your pint. The whole thing fits in a sentence: this tastes a bit vinegary to me, could you try it?

Which is the other reason to read a list like this one. Half of what is on it belongs somewhere, three of them belong in beers people pay a premium for, and knowing which is which is mostly a way of not sending back a beer that is doing exactly what it was built to do.

PINtPOINT records when a pub’s tap list was last confirmed. That is a dated sighting and not a measure of how the beer has been kept. What no tap list tells you, ours included, is when a line was last cleaned.
